questions.title: Purely sensory part of a spinal nerve
questions.question: Which part of a spinal nerve is formed of purely sensory fibres?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The ventral ramus lies distal to the union of the two roots, so like the whole spinal nerve trunk it is a mixed nerve, carrying both motor and sensory fibres, not purely sensory ones.
explanations.B: Correct. The dorsal (posterior) root is the one purely sensory component of a spinal nerve: it carries only afferent fibres, whose cell bodies sit in the dorsal root ganglion just before the root joins the ventral root. This sensory purity exists only at the root itself, proximal to the union that forms the mixed spinal nerve trunk -- once the roots unite, and again once the nerve splits into dorsal and ventral rami, motor and sensory fibres travel together. The companion question in this set asks for the purely motor part, which is the ventral root, the direct counterpart of this fact.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The ventral (anterior) root is the purely motor counterpart of the dorsal root, carrying only efferent fibres from the ventral grey horn -- the opposite of what this stem asks for.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Like the ventral ramus, the dorsal ramus lies distal to the union of the roots and is a mixed nerve, not a purely sensory one.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The nerve trunk is the mixed nerve formed after the dorsal and ventral roots unite, carrying both sensory and motor fibres together.

questions.learning_objective: State that the dorsal root of a spinal nerve is purely sensory.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.19 (rendered, row 1 = b)

questions.title: Purely motor part of a spinal nerve
questions.question: Which part of a spinal nerve is formed of purely motor fibres?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The ventral ramus lies distal to the union of the two roots, so it is a mixed nerve carrying both motor and sensory fibres, not purely motor ones.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The dorsal root is the purely sensory counterpart of the ventral root, carrying only afferent fibres -- the opposite of what this stem asks for.
explanations.C: Correct. The ventral (anterior) root is the one purely motor component of a spinal nerve: it carries only efferent fibres, arising from motor neurons in the ventral grey horn of the spinal cord. As with the dorsal root's sensory purity, this motor purity exists only at the root itself, proximal to the union that forms the mixed spinal nerve trunk. Preganglionic sympathetic fibres from thoracic segments travel out through this same ventral root, alongside the somatic motor fibres, before branching off separately further along the pathway.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Like the ventral ramus, the dorsal ramus lies distal to the union of the roots and is a mixed nerve, not a purely motor one.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The nerve trunk is the mixed nerve formed after the dorsal and ventral roots unite, carrying both motor and sensory fibres together.

questions.learning_objective: State that the ventral root of a spinal nerve is purely motor.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.19 (rendered, row 2 = c)

questions.title: Level of the sympathetic outflow
questions.question: The sympathetic outflow is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. No division of the autonomic outflow is described as purely cervical; the sympathetic preganglionic cell bodies begin no higher than the first thoracic segment.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Cranio-sacral describes the parasympathetic outflow, not the sympathetic one -- the two divisions leave the CNS at opposite levels.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Sacral segments (S2-S4) contribute to the parasympathetic outflow, not the sympathetic outflow.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Lumbo-sacral is not the recognised autonomic outflow level for either division; it conflates parts of both the sympathetic (lower thoracic to upper lumbar) and parasympathetic (sacral) ranges.
explanations.E: Correct. Preganglionic sympathetic neurons have their cell bodies in the lateral horn of the spinal cord from segment T1 down to about L2 or L3, which is why the sympathetic outflow is named thoraco-lumbar. This is the anatomical basis for contrasting it with the parasympathetic system's cranio-sacral outflow, from the brainstem cranial nerve nuclei and S2-S4. Confusing the two labels is one of the commonest errors in autonomic anatomy, since each name points to the exact opposite levels of the other division.

questions.learning_objective: State that the sympathetic outflow is thoraco-lumbar.

questions.title: Preganglionic sympathetic fibres in the thoracic spinal nerve
questions.question: Which part of a thoracic spinal nerve contains preganglionic sympathetic fibres?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The dorsal root carries only somatic sensory (afferent) fibres; sympathetic fibres are efferent and travel via the ventral, not dorsal, root.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The dorsal root ganglion houses the cell bodies of somatic sensory neurons, not preganglionic sympathetic neurons, whose cell bodies instead sit in the lateral horn of the spinal cord.
explanations.C: Correct. Preganglionic sympathetic neurons have their cell bodies in the lateral horn of the thoracolumbar spinal cord. Their axons leave the cord in the ventral root, alongside the somatic motor fibres, travel a short distance in the mixed spinal nerve trunk, and then branch off via the white ramus communicans to reach the sympathetic chain ganglion. At the level this question asks about -- the spinal nerve itself, before that branching -- the preganglionic sympathetic fibres are still inside the ventral root.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The dorsal ramus is a branch of the mixed spinal nerve trunk distal to where the sympathetic fibres would already have left via the white ramus communicans; it is not the structure carrying preganglionic sympathetic fibres at the level this question asks about.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The grey ramus communicans carries postganglionic, not preganglionic, sympathetic fibres, returning from the sympathetic chain ganglion back to the spinal nerve for distribution to the body wall and limbs.

questions.subtopic: Autonomic fibres in the spinal nerve
questions.learning_objective: Trace preganglionic sympathetic fibres through the ventral root of a thoracic spinal nerve.

questions.title: Level of the parasympathetic outflow
questions.question: The parasympathetic outflow is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. No division of the autonomic outflow is described as purely cervical.
explanations.B: Correct. The parasympathetic outflow leaves the CNS at two separate, non-contiguous levels: preganglionic fibres arise from the nuclei of cranial nerves III, VII, IX and X in the brainstem, and from the lateral grey matter of spinal cord segments S2-S4. Together these two sites give the outflow its name, cranio-sacral, distinguishing it from the sympathetic system's single continuous thoracolumbar band (T1 to L2/L3). Mixing up the two names -- assigning craniosacral to the sympathetic or thoracolumbar to the parasympathetic -- is a very common error precisely because they name opposite levels.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Sacral segments S2-S4 are only the caudal half of the parasympathetic outflow; the cranial nerve component is equally part of the definition, which is why the outflow is called cranio-sacral rather than simply sacral.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Lumbo-sacral is not the recognised parasympathetic outflow level; the sacral segments contribute, but the cranial nerve nuclei, not lumbar segments, provide the rostral component.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Thoraco-lumbar describes the sympathetic outflow, the opposite division from the one this stem asks about.

questions.learning_objective: State that the parasympathetic outflow is cranio-sacral.

questions.title: Correct statement about the nervous system
questions.question: As regards the nervous system, choose the correct statement:

options.A: Nerve plexuses are formed by dorsal rami of spinal nerves
options.B: Pia matter is the outermost one of the meninges
options.D: Ganglia are groups of nerve cells outside CNS
options.E: Ventral rami of spinal nerves are purely motor

explanations.A: Incorrect. Nerve plexuses (cervical, brachial, lumbar, sacral) are formed by the ventral rami of spinal nerves, not the dorsal rami, which instead supply the back segmentally without joining a plexus.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The pia mater is the innermost of the three meningeal layers, closely investing the neural tissue itself; the dura mater is the outermost layer.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The sympathetic system has a thoraco-lumbar outflow; cranio-sacral describes the parasympathetic system.
explanations.D: Correct. A ganglion is a group of nerve cell bodies located outside the central nervous system, in contrast to a nucleus, the equivalent grouping inside the CNS. Dorsal root ganglia (sensory) and autonomic ganglia (sympathetic chain, parasympathetic terminal ganglia) are all examples of this same structural category. This paired vocabulary -- ganglion outside the CNS, nucleus inside it -- is one of the basic organising distinctions of nervous system anatomy.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The ventral rami of spinal nerves are mixed nerves, carrying both motor and sensory fibres, not purely motor ones; it is only the ventral root, proximal to the rami, that is purely motor.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the true statement among common distractors about ganglia, plexus formation, the meninges and the ventral rami.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.19 (rendered, row 7 = d)

questions.title: Group of cell bodies in the PNS
questions.question: A group of nerve cell bodies located in the peripheral nervous system is called a:

explanations.A: Incorrect. A tract is a bundle of nerve fibres, not a group of cell bodies, and it lies within the CNS.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A nerve is a bundle of nerve fibres in the PNS, not a group of cell bodies.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A nucleus is the CNS equivalent of a ganglion -- a group of cell bodies, but located inside the central nervous system, not the PNS.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A synapse is the site of contact between two neurons, not a grouping of cell bodies.
explanations.E: Correct. A ganglion is a group of nerve cell bodies located outside the central nervous system -- the dorsal root ganglia and the sympathetic chain ganglia are examples. It is the direct PNS counterpart of a nucleus, the equivalent grouping inside the CNS, and this pairing (ganglion outside, nucleus inside) is one of five paired terms this question set tests across its matching block.

questions.learning_objective: Identify a ganglion as a group of nerve cell bodies located in the PNS.

questions.title: Group of cell bodies in the CNS
questions.question: A group of nerve cell bodies located in the central nervous system is called a:

explanations.A: Incorrect. A tract is a bundle of nerve fibres within the CNS, not a group of cell bodies.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A nerve is a bundle of nerve fibres in the PNS, the wrong location and the wrong structural category for this stem.
explanations.C: Correct. A nucleus is a group of nerve cell bodies located inside the central nervous system -- the cranial nerve nuclei of the brainstem and the basal ganglia's individual nuclei are examples, despite the confusingly similar name of the latter. It is the direct CNS counterpart of a ganglion, the equivalent grouping outside the CNS, tested from the opposite direction elsewhere in this same matching set.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A synapse is the site of contact between two neurons, not a grouping of cell bodies.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A ganglion is the PNS equivalent of a nucleus -- a group of cell bodies, but located outside the central nervous system, not inside it.

questions.learning_objective: Identify a nucleus as a group of nerve cell bodies located in the CNS.

questions.title: Bundle of nerve fibres in the CNS
questions.question: A bundle of nerve fibres located in the central nervous system is called a:

explanations.A: Correct. A tract is a bundle of nerve fibres running together within the central nervous system -- the corticospinal and spinothalamic tracts are examples. It is the direct CNS counterpart of a nerve, the equivalent fibre bundle outside the CNS, tested from the opposite direction elsewhere in this same matching set.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A nerve is a bundle of nerve fibres, but located in the PNS, not the CNS.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A nucleus is a group of cell bodies, not a bundle of fibres.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A synapse is the site of contact between two neurons, not a bundle of fibres.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A ganglion is a group of cell bodies located outside the CNS, not a bundle of fibres inside it.

questions.learning_objective: Identify a tract as a bundle of nerve fibres located in the CNS.

questions.title: Bundle of nerve fibres in the PNS
questions.question: A bundle of nerve fibres located in the peripheral nervous system is called a:

explanations.A: Incorrect. A tract is the CNS equivalent of a nerve -- a bundle of fibres, but located inside the central nervous system, not the PNS.
explanations.B: Correct. A nerve is a bundle of nerve fibres running together outside the central nervous system -- the median, radial and sciatic nerves are examples. It is the direct PNS counterpart of a tract, the equivalent fibre bundle inside the CNS.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A nucleus is a group of cell bodies, not a bundle of fibres.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A synapse is the site of contact between two neurons, not a bundle of fibres.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A ganglion is a group of cell bodies located outside the CNS, not a bundle of fibres.

questions.learning_objective: Identify a nerve as a bundle of nerve fibres located in the PNS.

questions.title: Site of contact between two neurons
questions.question: The site of contact between two neurons is called a:

explanations.A: Incorrect. A tract is a bundle of nerve fibres, not a point of contact between neurons.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A nerve is a bundle of nerve fibres, not a point of contact between neurons.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A nucleus is a group of cell bodies, not a point of contact between neurons.
explanations.D: Correct. A synapse is the site of functional contact between two neurons, where an electrical or chemical signal passes from a presynaptic to a postsynaptic cell. Unlike the other four terms in this matching set, which describe cell-body groupings (nucleus, ganglion) or fibre bundles (tract, nerve), a synapse describes a point of transmission, not a grouping or a bundle, wherever it happens to lie in the nervous system.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A ganglion is a group of cell bodies, not a point of contact between neurons.

questions.learning_objective: Identify a synapse as the site of contact between two neurons.

questions.title: Location of cerebrospinal fluid
questions.question: Cerebrospinal fluid lies between:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The space between the dura and arachnoid mater is the subdural space, a potential space that does not normally contain CSF.
explanations.B: Correct. Cerebrospinal fluid occupies the subarachnoid space, between the arachnoid mater and the pia mater, the innermost meningeal layer that closely invests the brain and spinal cord. This is the space a lumbar puncture needle must reach to sample CSF, and it is distinct from both the subdural space (dura to arachnoid) and the epidural space (external to the dura), neither of which normally contains CSF.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Dura and pia mater are not adjacent layers -- the arachnoid mater lies between them, and CSF occupies the subarachnoid space specifically between the arachnoid and the pia, not spanning all the way from dura to pia.
explanations.D: Incorrect. White matter and grey matter are regions of neural tissue itself, not a meningeal space, and CSF does not lie between them.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Option B (pia and arachnoid mater) correctly names the subarachnoid space where CSF lies, so "none of the above" is not correct.

questions.learning_objective: Locate cerebrospinal fluid in the subarachnoid space, between the arachnoid mater and the pia mater.

questions.title: Incorrect statement about spinal nerves
questions.question: As regards the spinal nerves, choose the INCORRECT statement:

options.A: Nerve plexuses are formed by dorsal rami of spinal nerves
options.B: Its dorsal roots are entirely sensory
options.E: Ventral rami of spinal nerves are mixed

explanations.A: Correct -- this is the incorrect statement. Nerve plexuses (cervical, brachial, lumbar, sacral) are formed by the ventral rami of spinal nerves, not the dorsal rami, which instead supply the skin and muscles of the back segmentally without contributing to a plexus. This is the false pairing this question is built to catch, restated from the opposite angle of the earlier "choose the correct statement" item in this set.
explanations.B: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is true, not the answer). The dorsal roots of spinal nerves are indeed entirely sensory, carrying only afferent fibres from the dorsal root ganglion.
explanations.C: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is true, not the answer). There are 31 pairs of spinal nerves: 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral and 1 coccygeal.
explanations.D: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is true, not the answer). The dorsal roots do carry ganglia -- the dorsal root ganglia, housing the cell bodies of the sensory neurons.
explanations.E: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is true, not the answer). The ventral rami of spinal nerves are indeed mixed, carrying both motor and sensory fibres, which is exactly what allows them (not the dorsal rami) to form functional plexuses supplying both movement and sensation.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the false statement among several true facts about spinal nerve roots, rami and plexus formation.

questions.title: Example of an anatomical end artery
questions.question: An example of an anatomical end artery is the:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The coronary arteries are the classic example of a functional, not anatomical, end artery -- they do have small collateral anastomoses, just ones ordinarily too narrow to prevent infarction after a sudden block.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The mesenteric arteries supply the gut via a rich marginal anastomotic arcade and are not considered end arteries of either type.
explanations.C: Correct. The cerebral arteries, at the level of their cortical branches, are a classic teaching example of an anatomical (true) end artery: their branches have no significant anastomotic connection with neighbouring cortical branches, which is exactly why occlusion of a cerebral artery branch produces a sharply demarcated infarct rather than a partially compensated one. The central retinal artery (option D) is also a genuine anatomical end artery in standard teaching, and either would be a defensible worked example of the same "no anastomosis at all" pattern -- the answer this bank marks for this item is the cerebral artery.
explanations.D: Incorrect for this item. The central retinal artery is a well recognised anatomical end artery, but the option this bank's printed key marks correct here is the cerebral artery; both illustrate the same principle.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The renal artery has some capsular and pelvic collateral anastomoses and is not the classic worked example of either end-artery type.

questions.learning_objective: Name the cerebral artery as a classic example of an anatomical end artery.

questions.title: Valve preventing backflow to the right atrium
questions.question: Which valve prevents the backward flow of blood into the right atrium?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The aortic valve is a semilunar valve preventing backflow from the aorta into the left ventricle, not into the right atrium.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The pulmonary valve is a semilunar valve preventing backflow from the pulmonary trunk into the right ventricle, one stage further along than the atrium this stem asks about.
explanations.C: Correct. The tricuspid valve is the right atrioventricular valve, guarding the opening between the right atrium and the right ventricle. During ventricular systole, rising pressure in the right ventricle closes its three cusps, preventing blood from regurgitating backward into the right atrium and directing it forward into the pulmonary trunk instead.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The tricuspid valve (option C) correctly answers this question, so "none of the above" is not correct.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The mitral valve performs the equivalent atrioventricular role on the left side of the heart, preventing backflow from the left ventricle into the left atrium, not the right atrium this stem asks about.

questions.learning_objective: State that the tricuspid valve prevents backflow of blood into the right atrium.

questions.title: Structure with no lymphatics
questions.question: Which one of the following structures has no lymphatics?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The pleura is well supplied with lymphatics, which drain the pleural space.
explanations.B: Correct. The central nervous system, including the brain, is a notable exception among vascular tissues: despite being highly vascular, it has no conventional lymphatic capillaries, and drains instead by other routes (perivascular and CSF pathways). This is distinct from the avascular tissues (cartilage, cornea, epidermis, nails), which lack lymphatics simply because they lack any blood supply at all -- the brain lacks lymphatics despite having one.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The intestine has abundant lymphatics, the lacteals, which are essential for absorbing dietary fat.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The dermis of the skin is well supplied with lymphatics; only the avascular epidermis above it lacks them.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The liver has lymphatics, in addition to being rich in blood sinusoids.

questions.learning_objective: State that the brain, despite being vascular, lacks conventional lymphatic capillaries.

field_notes.keySource: hand-marked answer in the original scan, rendered p.22 row 3 = b

questions.title: Example of a functional end artery
questions.question: An example of a functional end artery is the:

explanations.A: Correct. The coronary arteries are the classic example of a functional end artery: they do have small collateral anastomoses with neighbouring coronary branches, but these are ordinarily too narrow to carry an adequate blood supply if the main vessel is suddenly occluded, so a sudden block still causes myocardial infarction even though a channel technically exists. Gradual coronary narrowing, by contrast, may allow these same collaterals to enlarge and partially compensate -- the clinical basis for why chronic stable angina and acute occlusion behave so differently.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The mesenteric arteries supply the gut via a rich marginal anastomotic arcade and are not considered end arteries of either type.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The cerebral arteries are the classic worked example of an anatomical, not functional, end artery in this question set -- see the companion item testing that fact directly.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The central retinal artery is an anatomical end artery, with no anastomosis at all, not a functional one with small but insufficient collaterals.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The renal artery has some capsular and pelvic collateral anastomoses and is not the classic worked example of either end-artery type.

questions.learning_objective: Name the coronary artery as a classic example of a functional end artery.

questions.title: Path of the pulmonary circulation
questions.question: Pulmonary circulation includes the flow of blood from:

options.A: Left ventricle through aorta to body
options.B: Right ventricle through pulmonary trunk to lungs
options.C: Left atrium through left ventricle to aorta
options.D: Left ventricle through aorta to lungs
options.E: Right atrium through right ventricle to aorta

explanations.A: Incorrect. This describes a stage of the systemic circulation, carrying oxygenated blood from the left ventricle to the body, not the pulmonary circulation.
explanations.B: Correct. The pulmonary circulation is the low-pressure loop that carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle, through the pulmonary trunk and its two pulmonary arteries, to the lungs for gas exchange, before returning oxygenated blood to the left atrium via the pulmonary veins. This is the reverse of the naming convention many students expect: the pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood, and the pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood, the opposite pairing from the systemic circulation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This describes intracardiac flow on the left side of the heart, a stage of the systemic circulation, not the pulmonary circulation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The aorta is the great artery of the systemic circulation and does not carry blood to the lungs; this option also wrongly starts the pathway from the left ventricle.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The right atrium and right ventricle are correctly on the pulmonary side of the heart, but this option wrongly routes blood to the aorta rather than the pulmonary trunk and lungs.

questions.learning_objective: Trace the pulmonary circulation from the right ventricle through the pulmonary trunk to the lungs.

field_notes.keySource: hand-marked answer in the original scan, rendered p.22 row 5 = b

questions.title: Site lacking lymph capillaries
questions.question: Lymph capillaries are absent from:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Bone itself (as opposed to the avascular cartilage covering a joint surface) is vascular and does have lymphatics.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The stomach wall is well supplied with lymphatics, part of the gut's extensive lymphatic drainage.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The lungs have lymphatics, important both for fluid balance and as a route for the spread of lung cancer to hilar lymph nodes.
explanations.D: Correct. Articular cartilage is an avascular tissue: it has no blood supply of its own, relying instead on diffusion from the synovial fluid and underlying bone. Lymphatic capillaries normally follow blood capillaries into a tissue, so they are correspondingly absent from articular cartilage, along with the other avascular tissues such as the cornea, epidermis and nails.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The lips are richly vascular and lymphatic, which is also why arteriovenous anastomoses are numerous there for thermoregulation.

questions.learning_objective: State that articular cartilage, an avascular tissue, lacks lymphatic capillaries.

field_notes.keySource: hand-marked answer in the original scan, rendered p.22 row 6 = d

questions.title: Site rich in blood sinusoids
questions.question: Blood sinusoids are numerous in the:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Epiphyseal cartilage is avascular and contains no blood vessels of any kind, let alone sinusoids.
explanations.B: Correct. Sinusoids are wide, irregularly shaped vascular channels with a discontinuous or fenestrated lining, structurally intermediate between ordinary capillaries and small veins. They are most numerous in the liver, where hepatic sinusoids run between the plates of hepatocytes and are the organ's principal exchange vessels, permitting free passage of plasma proteins and blood cells that an ordinary capillary would not allow.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The cornea is avascular, relying on diffusion and the tear film for nutrition, and contains no blood sinusoids.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The epidermis is avascular and contains no blood vessels of any kind, let alone sinusoids.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The lips are richly vascular but via ordinary capillaries and arteriovenous anastomoses, not the wide sinusoidal channels characteristic of organs such as the liver.

questions.learning_objective: State that blood sinusoids are especially numerous in the liver.

field_notes.keySource: hand-marked answer in the original scan, rendered p.23 row 7 = b

questions.title: Circulation beginning and ending in capillaries
questions.question: The circulation that begins from capillaries and ends into capillaries is called:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The coronary circulation runs from the aorta through the coronary arteries, capillaries, and coronary veins/sinus back to the right atrium in a single pass, not through two separate capillary beds.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The cerebral circulation is a single-pass systemic-type circulation supplying brain tissue, not a portal-type circulation.
explanations.C: Correct. Most circulations run from arteries to capillaries to veins in a single pass, but a portal circulation is the exception: it begins in one set of capillaries, drains into a portal vein, and ends in a second set of capillaries before finally returning to the venous system. The hepatic portal circulation is the classic example -- blood from the intestinal capillary bed drains via the portal vein into the liver sinusoids, a second capillary-like bed, before leaving via the hepatic veins.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The systemic circulation runs from the left ventricle through the aorta, systemic capillaries, and veins back to the right atrium in a single pass, not through two capillary beds in series.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The pulmonary circulation runs from the right ventricle through the pulmonary arteries, pulmonary capillaries, and pulmonary veins to the left atrium in a single pass, not through two capillary beds in series.

questions.learning_objective: Define a portal circulation as one that begins and ends in a capillary bed.

field_notes.keySource: hand-marked answer in the original scan, rendered p.23 row 8 = c

questions.title: Consequence of lymphatic obstruction in the upper limb
questions.question: If the lymphatics of the upper limb become obstructed, the arm on that side is likely to:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Ischaemia results from a loss of arterial blood supply, not from a lymphatic blockage, which leaves the arterial supply untouched.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Hyperaemia is an increase in blood flow, not the fluid-accumulation consequence of lymphatic obstruction.
explanations.C: Correct. Lymphatic vessels normally return the protein-rich tissue fluid that capillaries filter out but do not fully reabsorb. When the lymphatics draining a limb become obstructed, this fluid can no longer be cleared and accumulates in the interstitial space, producing lymphoedema: firm, non-pitting swelling of the affected limb.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The opposite happens -- tissue fluid accumulates rather than being lost, because the lymphatics that would normally drain it away are blocked.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Obstructing the limb's lymphatic drainage produces a clear and clinically obvious change (oedema), not no change at all.

questions.learning_objective: State that lymphatic obstruction in a limb causes that limb to become oedematous.

questions.title: Site rich in arteriovenous anastomoses
questions.question: Arterio-venous anastomosis is frequently present in the:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The cornea is avascular and contains no blood vessels of any kind, let alone arteriovenous anastomoses.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Cartilage is avascular and contains no blood vessels of any kind.
explanations.C: Correct. Arteriovenous anastomoses are direct connections between an arteriole and a venule that bypass the intervening capillary bed, and the nail beds are one of their characteristic sites, alongside the skin of the nose and the lips. Opening or closing these anastomoses diverts blood flow near or away from the periphery and so plays a role in controlling body temperature and heat loss.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The epidermis is avascular and contains no blood vessels of any kind.
explanations.E: Incorrect for this item. The skin of the nose is also a genuine site rich in arteriovenous anastomoses, and would be an equally defensible answer to a differently worded stem -- the option this bank's printed key marks correct here is the nail beds.

questions.learning_objective: State that arteriovenous anastomoses are frequent in the nail beds, alongside the skin of the nose and lips.

field_notes.keySource: hand-marked answer in the original scan, rendered p.23 row 10 = c

questions.title: Vessel class with numerous valves
questions.question: Which class of vessel has numerous valves?

explanations.A: Incorrect. An arteriovenous anastomosis is a direct arteriole-venule connection, not the vessel class characteristically rich in valves.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Capillaries are simple, thin-walled exchange vessels with no valves at all.
explanations.C: Correct. Veins are the vessel class richest in valves, especially in the limbs. These valves prevent the backflow of blood under gravity and low venous pressure, helping propel blood towards the heart as surrounding muscles contract against them.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Arteries carry blood under high pulsatile pressure generated by the heart, and do not need or have valves along their course (aside from the semilunar valves at the roots of the great arteries).
explanations.E: Incorrect. Sinusoids are wide, irregular exchange vessels, particularly numerous in the liver, not the vessel class characteristically rich in valves.

questions.learning_objective: State that veins are the vessel class richest in valves.

field_notes.keySource: hand-marked answer in the original scan, rendered p.23 row 11 = c

questions.title: Abundant exchange vessels in the liver
questions.question: Which class of vessel is the abundant exchange vessel in the liver?

explanations.A: Incorrect. An arteriovenous anastomosis is a direct arteriole-venule connection, not an exchange vessel, and is not the liver's characteristic vessel type.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Ordinary capillaries are the universal exchange vessel present in most tissues, but the liver's own principal exchange vessels are the wider, more permeable sinusoids, not ordinary capillaries.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Veins are collecting vessels rich in valves, not exchange vessels.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Arteries are conducting vessels rich in elastic fibres, not exchange vessels.
explanations.E: Correct. Sinusoids are wide, irregular vascular channels with a discontinuous or fenestrated lining, structurally intermediate between capillaries and small veins. They are the liver's principal exchange vessels, running between the plates of hepatocytes and permitting free passage of plasma proteins and even blood cells that an ordinary capillary would not allow.

questions.learning_objective: Identify sinusoids as the liver's abundant exchange vessel.

questions.title: Exchange vessels present in all tissues
questions.question: Which class of vessel is the exchange vessel present in all tissues?

explanations.A: Incorrect. An arteriovenous anastomosis is a direct arteriole-venule bypass route, not the universal exchange vessel.
explanations.B: Correct. Capillaries are the true exchange vessels, present in essentially every vascularised tissue, where their thin single-cell wall permits the exchange of gases, nutrients and waste between blood and tissue. Unlike sinusoids, which are wider, more permeable, and concentrated in specific organs such as the liver, ordinary capillaries are the general-purpose exchange vessel found almost everywhere blood flows.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Veins are collecting vessels rich in valves, not exchange vessels.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Arteries are conducting vessels rich in elastic fibres, not exchange vessels.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Sinusoids are specialised, wider exchange vessels concentrated in particular organs (the liver especially), not the universal exchange vessel present in every tissue.

questions.learning_objective: State that capillaries are the exchange vessel present in all tissues.

field_notes.keySource: hand-marked answer in the original scan, rendered p.23 row 13 = b

questions.title: Vessel class rich in elastic fibres
questions.question: Which class of vessel is rich in elastic fibres?

explanations.A: Incorrect. An arteriovenous anastomosis is a direct arteriole-venule connection, not characterised by elastic-fibre richness.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Capillaries have only a thin single-cell wall, with no significant elastic fibre content.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Veins are richer in valves than in elastic fibres, and have a thinner, less elastic wall than arteries carrying the same calibre of blood.
explanations.D: Correct. Arteries, especially the larger elastic arteries near the heart, are richest in elastic fibres within their wall. This lets them distend during systole and recoil during diastole, smoothing the heart's pulsatile output into a steadier stream by the time blood reaches the capillaries.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Sinusoids are wide, irregular, thin-walled exchange vessels, not vessels characterised by elastic-fibre richness.

questions.learning_objective: State that arteries are the vessel class richest in elastic fibres.

questions.title: Vessel class controlling body temperature
questions.question: Which class of vessel plays a role in controlling body temperature?

explanations.A: Correct. Arteriovenous anastomoses are direct connections between an arteriole and a venule that bypass the capillary bed, numerous in the skin of the nose, nail beds and lips. Opening or closing them diverts blood flow near or away from the skin surface, and this rapid, valve-like diversion is what allows them to play a specific role in controlling body temperature and heat loss.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Capillaries are the general exchange vessel of the tissues, not a specialised thermoregulatory route.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Veins are collecting vessels rich in valves, not a specialised thermoregulatory route.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Arteries are conducting vessels rich in elastic fibres, not a specialised thermoregulatory route.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Sinusoids are wide exchange vessels concentrated in organs such as the liver, not a thermoregulatory structure of the skin.

questions.learning_objective: State that arteriovenous anastomoses play a role in controlling body temperature.

questions.title: Circulation connecting two sets of capillaries
questions.question: The circulation that connects two sets of capillaries is called:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The systemic circulation runs from the left ventricle through the aorta, systemic capillaries, and veins back to the right atrium in a single pass, not through two capillary beds in series.
explanations.B: Correct. A portal circulation begins in one set of capillaries, drains into a portal vein, and ends in a second set of capillaries before returning to the venous system -- the defining feature that separates it from every other circulation type. The hepatic portal circulation, running from the intestinal capillary bed through the portal vein to the liver sinusoids, is the classic example of this two-capillary-bed arrangement.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The pulmonary circulation runs from the right ventricle through the pulmonary arteries, pulmonary capillaries, and pulmonary veins to the left atrium in a single pass, not through two capillary beds in series.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Only the portal circulation connects two sets of capillaries in series; the systemic and pulmonary circulations do not, so "all of the above" is not correct.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The portal circulation (option B) correctly answers this question, so "none of the above" is not correct.

questions.learning_objective: Identify a portal circulation as the type that connects two sets of capillaries.

field_notes.keySource: hand-marked answer in the original scan, rendered p.23 row 16 = b

questions.title: Routes of communication between arteries and veins
questions.question: Communication between arteries and veins in the tissues can be by:

options.A: Direct connection between arterioles and venules

explanations.A: Incorrect on its own -- true, but not the complete answer. A direct arteriole-to-venule connection (an arteriovenous anastomosis) is one genuine route of communication, but it is not the only one, so this option alone is incomplete.
explanations.B: Incorrect on its own -- true, but not the complete answer. Ordinary capillaries are the most common route linking arteries and veins in virtually every tissue, but again this is only one of several valid routes.
explanations.C: Incorrect on its own -- true, but not the complete answer. Cavernous, erectile-type vascular tissue (as in the penis or nasal turbinates) is a further genuine route of arteriovenous communication, but not the only one.
explanations.D: Incorrect on its own -- true, but not the complete answer. Sinusoids, particularly in organs such as the liver, also link the arterial and venous sides of the circulation, but this too is only one of several valid routes.
explanations.E: Correct. Communication between arteries and veins in the tissues can occur through several distinct routes: direct arteriovenous anastomoses, ordinary capillaries, cavernous erectile-type tissue, and sinusoids. Each route serves a different structural and functional purpose -- the direct anastomosis is the fastest-acting, valve-like route dedicated to thermoregulation, while capillaries are the universal exchange route and sinusoids are the specialised high-permeability route of organs such as the liver -- so recognising all four together, not any single one, is the complete answer.

questions.learning_objective: List the routes of communication between arteries and veins: direct anastomosis, capillaries, cavernous tissue and sinusoids.

field_notes.keySource: hand-marked answer in the original scan, rendered p.24 row 17 = e

questions.title: Incorrect statement about blood vessels
questions.question: Choose the INCORRECT statement:

options.C: Portal circulation possesses two sets of capillaries
options.D: Arteries carry the blood away from the heart

explanations.A: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is true, not the answer). Veins of the limbs are indeed richly supplied with valves, which prevent backflow of blood under gravity.
explanations.B: Correct -- this is the incorrect statement. Convention gives arteries and veins different descriptive vocabulary: an artery gives off branches, while a vein receives tributaries, reflecting the opposite direction of flow -- away from the heart in an artery, toward it in a vein. Describing veins as having "branches" is the deliberately wrong swap this question is built to catch.
explanations.C: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is true, not the answer). The portal circulation does possess two sets of capillaries in series -- the defining feature that separates it from other circulation types.
explanations.D: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is true, not the answer). Arteries do carry blood away from the heart, by definition.
explanations.E: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is true, not the answer). Some arteries are indeed tortuous (coiled or winding) in their course, such as the facial or uterine arteries, an adaptation that accommodates movement or growth of the structures they supply.

questions.learning_objective: Identify that veins have tributaries, not branches, as the false statement among true facts about vessels.

questions.title: Incorrect statement about anastomoses
questions.question: As regards anastomoses, choose the INCORRECT statement:

options.A: Arterio-venous anastomoses are numerous in skin of nose
options.B: Anatomical end artery has no anastomosis with other arteries
options.C: Arterio-venous anastomosis helps to control body temperature
options.D: Arterial anastomosis helps to compensate a block in blood flow
options.E: Functional end arteries are sufficient to compensate a block of an artery

explanations.A: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is true, not the answer). Arteriovenous anastomoses are indeed numerous in the skin of the nose, one of their characteristic thermoregulatory sites.
explanations.B: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is true, not the answer). An anatomical (true) end artery, by definition, has no anastomotic connection with neighbouring arteries at all.
explanations.C: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is true, not the answer). Arteriovenous anastomoses do help control body temperature, by diverting blood flow near or away from the skin surface.
explanations.D: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is true, not the answer). Ordinary arterial anastomoses -- as opposed to a functional end artery's sparse collaterals -- can indeed enlarge over time to compensate for a gradual block in blood flow, providing a collateral route around an obstruction.
explanations.E: Correct -- this is the incorrect statement. A functional end artery, such as a coronary artery, does have small collateral anastomoses, but these are ordinarily too narrow to carry an adequate blood supply if the main vessel is suddenly occluded. Functional end arteries are therefore not sufficient to compensate a sudden block -- infarction still occurs -- which is exactly what separates a functional end artery from an ordinary artery with a genuinely adequate anastomotic network.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that a functional end artery's collaterals are not sufficient to compensate a sudden arterial block.

field_notes.keySource: hand-marked answer in the original scan, rendered p.24 row 19 = e

questions.title: Incorrect statement about blood vessels
questions.question: As regards blood vessels, choose the INCORRECT statement:

options.D: Valves are numerous in limb veins

explanations.A: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is true, not the answer). Arteries do give off branches, by convention, reflecting the direction of flow away from the heart.
explanations.B: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is true, not the answer). Veins do receive tributaries, by convention, reflecting the direction of flow toward the heart.
explanations.C: Correct -- this is the incorrect statement. Venae comitantes are paired small veins that run alongside, and drain, a small or medium-sized artery -- the radial and ulnar arteries are classic examples -- not a big vein. Pairing venae comitantes with a big vein, as this option does, is the deliberately wrong swap this question is built to catch.
explanations.D: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is true, not the answer). Valves are indeed numerous in limb veins, preventing backflow of blood under gravity.
explanations.E: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is true, not the answer). Sinusoids, being wide and irregular with a more tortuous course than an ordinary capillary, do slow down blood flow, which is part of what allows the extended contact time needed for their exchange function.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that venae comitantes accompany a small or medium artery, not a big vein, as the false statement among true facts.

questions.title: Sites lacking lymph capillaries, taken together
questions.question: Lymph capillaries are absent in:

explanations.A: Incorrect on its own -- true, but not the complete answer. Avascular structures genuinely lack lymph capillaries, since lymphatics normally follow blood capillaries into a tissue, but this is only one category among several named here.
explanations.B: Incorrect on its own -- true, but not the complete answer. Articular cartilage, itself an avascular tissue, does lack lymph capillaries, but it is only one specific example among the options listed.
explanations.C: Incorrect on its own -- true, but not the complete answer. Nails, another avascular structure, do lack lymph capillaries, but again this is only one example among the options listed.
explanations.D: Incorrect on its own -- true, but not the complete answer. The central nervous system lacks lymph capillaries despite being vascular, a separate exception from the avascular tissues, but this too is only one option among those listed.
explanations.E: Correct. Lymph capillaries are absent from all four of the categories named here: avascular structures generally, articular cartilage and nails specifically as worked examples of avascular tissue, and the central nervous system as a further, separate exception that lacks lymphatics despite being highly vascular. Recognising all of them together, not any single one, is the complete answer this question tests.

questions.learning_objective: List the tissue types that lack lymph capillaries: avascular structures generally, cartilage, nails, and the CNS.

questions.title: Defining property of lymph capillaries
questions.question: Lymph capillaries:

options.B: Are present in all tissues of body
options.C: Are permeable to small particles only
options.D: Are smaller in caliber than blood capillaries

explanations.A: Correct. Unlike blood capillaries, which connect an arteriole to a venule at both ends, lymph capillaries begin as blind-ended tubes within the tissue spaces, open only at their proximal end where they drain into larger collecting lymphatics. This blind origin is their single most distinguishing structural feature and is universally true of them, unlike the other options offered here, each of which has genuine exceptions.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Lymph capillaries are not present in every tissue of the body -- they are absent from avascular tissues, the central nervous system, and bone marrow, among others -- so this is not a universally true statement.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Lymph capillaries are in fact more permeable than blood capillaries, admitting larger molecules, proteins, and even cells that a blood capillary's wall would not allow through; "small particles only" understates their permeability rather than describing it accurately.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Lymph capillaries are generally similar in calibre to, or even slightly larger and more irregular than, blood capillaries, not smaller.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Only option A is universally true of lymph capillaries; options B, C and D each have genuine exceptions, so "all the above" is not correct.

questions.learning_objective: State that lymph capillaries characteristically start blindly, distinguishing this universal property from options that have real exceptions.

field_notes.keySource: hand-marked answer in the original scan, rendered p.25 row 24 = a

questions.title: Incorrect statement about lymph vessels
questions.question: As regards lymph vessels, choose the INCORRECT statement:

options.D: All of them end in thoracic duct
options.E: Are interrupted by one or more lymph nodes

explanations.A: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is true, not the answer). Lymph vessels do contain numerous valves along their course, which keep lymph flowing in one direction, toward the venous system.
explanations.B: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is true, not the answer). Lymph vessels do typically accompany veins along much of their course.
explanations.C: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is true, not the answer). Lymph vessels do ultimately drain into the venous system, at the venous angles at the root of the neck.
explanations.D: Correct -- this is the incorrect statement. Most of the body's lymph drains via the thoracic duct into the left venous angle, but the right upper limb, the right side of the head and neck, and the right side of the thorax instead drain via the separate right lymphatic duct into the right venous angle. Claiming that "all" lymph vessels end in the thoracic duct overlooks this separate right-sided route.
explanations.E: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is true, not the answer). Lymph vessels are indeed interrupted by one or more lymph nodes along their course, where lymph is filtered and immune surveillance occurs.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that not all lymph vessels drain via the thoracic duct, naming the right lymphatic duct as the separate route.
